name: Cybersecurity 101
author: Recurse
subject: security
description: Core security for everyone: CIA triad, phishing, malware, passwords and MFA, injection, least privilege, patching and response.

lesson.intro: Security is everyone's job, from the developer writing a login form to the employee reading an email. This lesson builds the core mental models: what we protect (the CIA triad), how attackers get in (social engineering, malware and injection), and the habits that stop them: strong authentication, least privilege, patching, logging and layered defenses.
objectives: Classify incidents with the CIA triad and tell threats, vulnerabilities and risk apart
Recognize phishing, social engineering and the main kinds of malware, and the defenses against each
Explain authentication versus authorization, MFA factors and safe password practice
Describe how SQL injection and XSS work and how parameterized queries and output escaping stop them
Apply least privilege, patching, logging, incident response and defense in depth

sections.title: The CIA triad, threats and risk
sections.body:
A hospital's patient records leak online. A ransomware gang locks the same hospital's systems for a week. An insider quietly changes medication doses in the database. All three are security failures, but each breaks something different, and security people describe them with the **CIA triad**:

- **Confidentiality**: only authorized people can read the data. Broken by a data leak, a stolen laptop or someone reading traffic on public Wi-Fi.
- **Integrity**: data and systems are not changed without authorization, and changes can be detected. Broken by tampered records or a modified software update.
- **Availability**: systems and data are there when needed. Broken by ransomware, a denial-of-service (DoS) attack or a failed server with no backup.

Every security control protects one or more of these. Encryption mostly protects confidentiality, hashes and digital signatures protect integrity, and backups and redundancy protect availability.

Four words get mixed up constantly, so pin them down:

- A **vulnerability** is a weakness: an unpatched bug, a default password, an employee who has never seen a phishing email.
- A **threat** is someone or something that could cause harm: a criminal gang, a careless insider, a flood.
- An **exploit** is the specific technique or code that takes advantage of a vulnerability.
- **Risk** combines how **likely** it is that a threat exploits a vulnerability with how bad the **impact** would be.

Security work is mostly risk management. Nobody can fix everything, so organizations rank risks and choose a response for each: **reduce** it with controls, **transfer** it (insurance, outsourcing), **avoid** it (stop doing the risky thing) or **accept** it. Some controls cut likelihood, like MFA, which makes a stolen password far less useful. Others cut impact, like backups, which turn a ransomware disaster into a bad day.

Attackers range from automated bots scanning the whole internet for known flaws, through criminal groups after money, to insiders and well-funded state actors. Most attacks on ordinary organizations are opportunistic: they hit whoever has the unpatched server or the reused password. The sum of every way in (every exposed service, login page and person who can be tricked) is the **attack surface**.
sections.code:
Confidentiality
          (only the right people read it)
                      /\
                     /  \
                    /    \
                   /______\
        Integrity            Availability
(no unauthorized changes)    (there when needed)

Risk = likelihood x impact
sections.pitfall: Treating security as only keeping secrets. Ransomware attacks availability first, which is why backups count as a security control.

check.question: A denial-of-service attack floods an online store until customers cannot load it. Which part of the CIA triad is under attack?
choices: Confidentiality
Integrity
Availability
Authentication
check.explanation: Nothing is read or changed; the service simply cannot be used, which is availability. Authentication is a security mechanism, not one of the three goals.

sections.title: Phishing and social engineering
sections.body:
Most breaches do not start with a brilliant hack. They start with a person being tricked. **Social engineering** manipulates people into giving away access, money or information, and it works because it targets trust, fear and helpfulness rather than software bugs.

**Phishing** is the email version: a message that looks like it comes from a bank, a delivery company or IT, with a link to a fake login page or a malicious attachment. Its relatives:

- **Spear phishing** targets one person or team using real details, such as their manager's name or a current project. Aimed at executives, it is called **whaling**.
- **Smishing** (text messages) and **vishing** (voice calls) use the same tricks over other channels.
- **Business email compromise** (BEC) impersonates an executive or supplier to get a payment sent to the attacker's account, often from a real, hijacked mailbox.
- **Pretexting** builds a believable story first: "I'm the new contractor and my badge isn't working yet."

The red flags are about pressure and mismatch, not spelling mistakes, which AI tools have largely removed:

- **Urgency or fear**: "your account will be closed in one hour".
- **A request to skip the normal process**: pay a new bank account, read out an MFA code, buy gift cards.
- **A mismatch** between who the message claims to be and where it really comes from or links to.

Checking a link means reading its real domain: the part just before the first single `/`, read from the right. `https://login.example-bank.com/` belongs to `example-bank.com`, but `https://example-bank.com.secure-login.net/` belongs to `secure-login.net`.

The reliable defense is to **verify through a channel you already trust**: hang up and call the number on your bank card, look up the supplier's phone number yourself, type the address instead of clicking. Organizations add technical layers (spam filtering, email authentication with SPF, DKIM and DMARC, phishing-resistant MFA) and a culture where reporting a suspicious message is praised, even when it turns out to be harmless.
sections.code:
From:    "IT Service Desk" <it-support@examp1e-corp.com>
Subject: URGENT: your password expires in 60 minutes

Your password expires today. To keep access to email and payroll,
confirm your credentials now:

    https://example-corp.com.account-verify.net/login

Red flags: a lookalike sender domain (examp1e, with a digit 1),
urgency, and a link whose real domain is account-verify.net
sections.pitfall: Trusting a message because it contains correct internal details or comes from a real colleague's address. Attackers research targets and hijack real mailboxes; verify unusual requests out of band.

check.question: A text from your "bank" says a payment is blocked and asks you to log in through a link. What is the safest response?
choices: Click the link, but check for the padlock icon first
Open the bank's app or type its address yourself, ignoring the link
Reply STOP to show you are not interested
Forward it to friends to warn them, then click it
check.explanation: Going to the bank through a route you already trust means a fake link cannot fool you. Phishing sites have valid padlocks for their own domains, and replying confirms your number is active.

sections.title: Malware
sections.body:
**Malware** is any software written to harm a system or its owner. It is grouped by how it spreads and what it does:

- A **virus** attaches itself to legitimate files or programs and spreads when they are run or shared.
- A **worm** spreads by itself across networks, usually through an unpatched service, with no user action. Worms can hit thousands of machines in hours.
- A **trojan** pretends to be something useful, like a free game or a cracked app, so the victim installs it willingly.
- **Ransomware** encrypts files and demands payment for the key. Modern gangs also steal data first and threaten to publish it (double extortion).
- **Spyware** and **keyloggers** secretly collect information, from browsing habits to every password typed.
- A **rootkit** hides deep in the system, often in the kernel, to conceal itself and other malware.
- A **botnet** is a network of infected machines under an attacker's remote control, used for spam, DDoS attacks and credential stuffing.

The categories overlap. WannaCry, in 2017, was ransomware that spread like a worm through a Windows file-sharing (SMB) flaw that had been patched two months earlier.

Malware gets in through a handful of doors: phishing attachments and links, malicious downloads and browser extensions, unpatched internet-facing services, infected USB drives and stolen remote-access credentials. Closing those doors is most of the defense:

- Keep systems and software **patched**, which shuts the doors worms use.
- Run **endpoint protection** (modern antivirus and EDR, endpoint detection and response) that watches behavior, not just known signatures.
- Apply **least privilege**, so malware running as an ordinary user cannot take over the whole machine.
- Keep **backups** that ransomware cannot reach, following the **3-2-1 rule**: three copies of your data, on two different types of storage, with one copy offsite or offline. Test restores regularly, because an untested backup is a hope, not a plan.

A folder that syncs instantly to the cloud is not a backup on its own: when ransomware encrypts your files, the sync faithfully uploads the encrypted versions.
sections.pitfall: Relying on antivirus alone. New malware can evade detection for days; patching, least privilege and offline backups limit the damage when something gets through.

check.question: Malware disguised as a free PDF editor, which users download and install themselves, is best described as:
choices: A worm
A rootkit
A botnet
A trojan
check.explanation: A trojan gets in by looking useful, so the victim installs it. A worm spreads with no user action, and rootkits and botnets describe hiding and remote control, not how the malware arrived.

sections.title: Authentication, passwords and MFA
sections.body:
Every login answers two separate questions. **Authentication** asks "who are you?" and checks proof such as a password. **Authorization** asks "what are you allowed to do?" once the system knows who you are. A logged-in employee refused the payroll page passed authentication and failed authorization. On the web the two map to different errors: 401 means "we do not know who you are", 403 means "we know, and the answer is no".

Proof of identity comes in **factors**:

- Something you **know**: a password or PIN.
- Something you **have**: a phone with an authenticator app, a hardware security key.
- Something you **are**: a fingerprint or face.

**Multi-factor authentication** (MFA) requires factors of different kinds, so a stolen password alone is not enough. A password plus a security question is still one factor (two things you know). Not all MFA is equal: SMS codes can be stolen by SIM swapping, push notifications can be approved by a tired user who is spammed with requests (**MFA fatigue**), and both codes and pushes can be relayed by a real-time phishing site. **Passkeys** and FIDO2 security keys are **phishing-resistant**: the browser completes the login only for the genuine site's domain, so a lookalike site gets nothing.

Passwords are still everywhere, so use them well:

- **Length beats complexity.** A long passphrase of random words is stronger and easier to remember than `P@ssw0rd!`, whose substitutions attackers try first.
- **Never reuse a password.** Attackers take email and password pairs leaked from one breach and try them on other sites, an attack called **credential stuffing**.
- Use a **password manager** to generate and store a unique password for every site. It also refuses to autofill on a lookalike domain, a quiet anti-phishing bonus.

If you build a login system, never store passwords, not even encrypted. Store a **salted, slow password hash** from a function designed for it, such as Argon2, bcrypt or scrypt. A unique random salt per user makes identical passwords produce different hashes, and the deliberate slowness turns billions of guesses per second into thousands. A fast hash such as MD5 or plain SHA-256 is the wrong tool.
sections.code:
from argon2 import PasswordHasher
from argon2.exceptions import VerifyMismatchError

ph = PasswordHasher()

# Sign-up: store only the hash. A random salt is generated and embedded in it.
stored = ph.hash("correct horse battery staple")
# stored looks like: $argon2id$v=19$m=65536,t=3,p=4$<salt>$<hash>

# Login: check an attempt against the stored hash
try:
    ph.verify(stored, "correct horse battery staple")
    print("Welcome back")
except VerifyMismatchError:
    print("Wrong password")
sections.pitfall: Approving an MFA prompt you did not start. A request you did not trigger means someone already has your password; deny it and change the password.

activity.title: 401 versus 403
activity.prompt: Call the protected endpoint without a token, log in, call it again with your token, then try the admin endpoint. Read each status code: 401 is a failed authentication (who are you?), 403 a failed authorization (you may not).

check.question: Why is a long passphrase like `maple-orbit-tunnel-crayon` usually stronger than `P@ssw0rd!`?
choices: Its length creates far more possibilities than symbol swaps, which crackers try first
Hyphens are special characters that cracking tools cannot handle
Dictionary words cannot be guessed by computers
Short passwords are stored with weaker hashes by websites
check.explanation: Four randomly chosen words from a large list give an enormous number of combinations, while common substitutions like @ for a and 0 for o are built into every cracking tool. The strength comes from randomness and length, not from the words being secret.

sections.title: Attacks on web apps: injection and XSS
sections.body:
Two bug classes have topped web security lists for decades, and both come from the same mistake: letting **data** from a user be treated as **code**.

**SQL injection** happens when a program builds a query by pasting user input into the SQL text. Take a login lookup written as `f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'"`. If someone types `' OR '1'='1` as the name, the query becomes `... WHERE name = '' OR '1'='1'`, which is true for every row. Nastier inputs read other tables or delete data. The fix is **parameterized queries** (prepared statements): the SQL text holds placeholders and the values travel separately, so the database never parses them as SQL. Every database library supports them, and ORMs use them by default. Escaping input by hand or blocking "bad characters" is fragile and no substitute.

**Cross-site scripting** (XSS) is the same mistake in the browser. If a page inserts user input into HTML without escaping it, an attacker can supply a `<script>` that runs in other users' browsers, on your site's origin, where it can read the page, act as the user or steal tokens. **Stored** XSS saves the payload, for example in a comment, and hits everyone who views it; **reflected** XSS bounces it off a URL parameter in a link the victim is tricked into opening. The fix is **output encoding**: escape `<`, `>`, `&` and quotes for the context you are writing into, which template engines such as Jinja and React do by default. A **Content-Security-Policy** header adds a second layer by telling the browser which scripts may run.

The same pattern explains **command injection** (user input pasted into a shell command) and **path traversal** (`../../etc/passwd` used as a file name). The general rule: never trust input, keep code and data apart with safe APIs, and validate input against what you expect (an order ID should be a number) as an extra layer, not the only one.

Two more attacks round out the basics. **Denial of service** (DoS, or DDoS when a botnet does it) overwhelms a service until real users cannot reach it. An **on-path** (man-in-the-middle) attacker sits between two parties to read or alter their traffic, which is exactly what TLS with certificate checking prevents.
sections.code:
import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect("shop.db")
cur = conn.cursor()
name = input("Name: ")          # an attacker types: ' OR '1'='1

# Vulnerable: the input becomes part of the SQL text
cur.execute(f"SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'")

# Safe: a placeholder, with the value passed separately
cur.execute("SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE name = ?", (name,))
sections.pitfall: Trying to block attacks by filtering quotes or words like SELECT. Attackers have endless encodings; parameterized queries and output escaping remove the problem instead of chasing it.

activity.title: See the injected query
activity.prompt: Run it and read the final SQL: the input has become part of the query's logic. Then try the DROP TABLE input from the comment. A parameterized query never builds this string at all, which is why it is the real fix.

props.code:
name = "' OR '1'='1"

query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'"
print(query)

# Try another input, then run again:
# name = "x'; DROP TABLE users; --"
props.task: Set name to the DROP TABLE input and read the query it produces.

check.question: What is the most reliable fix for SQL injection?
choices: Removing apostrophes from all user input
Hiding database error messages from users
Running every query inside a try block
Parameterized queries that send values separately from the SQL
check.explanation: With parameters, the database receives the SQL and the values separately, so input can never change the query's structure. Stripping characters misses other encodings, and hiding errors only makes attacks quieter.

sections.title: Least privilege and access control
sections.body:
An intern's laptop gets malware. If the intern's account can reach only their team's shared folder, the damage is one folder. If it is a domain administrator because "it was easier", the attacker owns the company. The difference is **least privilege**: every person, program and service gets the minimum access it needs to do its job, and no more, for no longer than needed.

In practice:

- **Separate admin accounts.** Administrators use an ordinary account for email and browsing, and a separate privileged account only for admin work, so a phishing link opened from the everyday account cannot use admin rights.
- **Role-based access control** (RBAC): grant permissions to roles such as "support agent" or "billing admin", then assign people to roles. When someone changes jobs, you change their role instead of untangling individual grants.
- **Service accounts** get only what the application does. A web shop that reads products and writes orders gets exactly those rights, not database admin. Cloud permissions follow the same idea: a backup job that writes to one storage bucket may write to that bucket, not do everything everywhere.
- **Just-in-time access**: elevate only when needed (`sudo` for one command, a time-limited admin role) instead of holding standing privileges.
- **Separation of duties**: no single person can both create a new supplier and approve payments to it, so fraud requires collusion.
- **Access reviews and fast offboarding**: accounts of people who left, and permissions nobody remembers granting, are favorite ways in.

Least privilege limits the **blast radius**. It does not stop the first compromise, but it decides whether an incident is a nuisance or a catastrophe, and it slows an attacker trying to move from system to system (**lateral movement**). It also contains honest mistakes: an account that cannot delete production data cannot delete it by accident either.
sections.pitfall: Granting broad permissions "temporarily" to get something working and never removing them. Temporary admin rights tend to become permanent; set an expiry or a reminder.

check.question: Which of these is the best example of least privilege?
choices: Every developer has admin rights on production to fix bugs quickly
The whole IT team shares one admin password
A reporting tool has read-only access to the sales tables it reports on
A service account gets full rights so it never hits permission errors
check.explanation: The reporting tool can do exactly its job and nothing else, so a compromise or bug in it cannot change data. The other options hand out far more power than the job needs, and a shared password also destroys accountability.

sections.title: Patching and hardening
sections.body:
In 2017 attackers stole personal data on about 147 million people from the credit bureau Equifax through a flaw in the Apache Struts web framework, for which a patch had been available for about two months. Most successful attacks use **known** vulnerabilities, not exotic new ones, which makes patching one of the most valuable security habits there is.

Vulnerabilities are catalogued as **CVEs** (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures), each with an ID such as `CVE-2021-44228` (the Log4Shell bug) and usually a **CVSS** severity score from 0 to 10. A **zero-day** is a flaw attackers exploit before the vendor has a fix. Once a patch exists, the race is between defenders applying it and attackers scanning the internet for systems that have not.

You cannot patch everything at once, so prioritize by risk:

- **Actively exploited** vulnerabilities first. Lists such as CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog exist for exactly this.
- **Internet-facing** systems before internal ones: VPNs, firewalls, web servers and email gateways are scanned constantly.
- Then severity, and how important the system is.

Good patch management is a routine, not a heroic weekend: an inventory of what you run (you cannot patch what you do not know about), automatic updates where safe, testing for critical systems and a deadline for each severity level. Include dependencies: your application's libraries need updates just like the operating system, and tools such as `npm audit`, `pip-audit` and Dependabot flag vulnerable ones.

**Hardening** shrinks the attack surface before anything goes wrong:

- Change or disable **default passwords** and accounts.
- Turn off services, ports and features that are not needed; every listening service is a possible way in.
- Use secure configurations: SSH with keys instead of passwords, no direct root login, TLS everywhere.
- Remove software nobody uses, and replace systems that are **end of life** and no longer receive security updates.
sections.code:
$ sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade   # patch a Debian or Ubuntu server
$ npm audit                             # check a project's JavaScript dependencies
$ pip-audit                             # the same for Python dependencies

$ sudo ss -tlnp                         # which services are listening? (trimmed)
LISTEN  0.0.0.0:22     users:(("sshd",pid=812))
LISTEN  0.0.0.0:443    users:(("nginx",pid=930))
LISTEN  0.0.0.0:3306   users:(("mysqld",pid=1044))   # database open to every network?
sections.pitfall: Patching the operating system but never the application's dependencies. A library such as Log4j can be the open door on an otherwise fully updated server.

check.question: What is a CVE?
choices: A public identifier for one specific known vulnerability
A type of malware that targets web servers
A firewall rule that blocks known attackers
A score from 0 to 10 for how costly an attack is
check.explanation: A CVE ID such as CVE-2021-44228 names one vulnerability so that vendors, scanners and defenders all refer to the same thing. The 0 to 10 severity score is a separate system, CVSS.

sections.title: Logging, incident response and defense in depth
sections.body:
Sooner or later something gets through. What separates a contained incident from a disaster is whether you notice quickly and know what to do next. Attackers often stay unnoticed inside networks for weeks, and logs are how you shorten that.

**Logging** basics:

- Record **security-relevant events**: logins and failed logins, permission changes, admin actions, access to sensitive data, and patterns such as a burst of 401s from one address.
- Include context: a timestamp from a synchronized clock (NTP), the user, the source IP and what happened.
- Never log secrets: passwords, full card numbers, session tokens.
- Send logs to a **central** system, often a SIEM (security information and event management), where they can be searched, correlated and alerted on. An attacker who gains admin on a server can wipe its local logs, but not copies already shipped elsewhere.

**Incident response** is a plan you write before you need it. A widely used model from NIST moves through these phases:

- **Preparation**: contacts, tools, backups, a written plan and practice drills.
- **Detection and analysis**: notice the alert, confirm it is real, work out the scope.
- **Containment**: stop the spread, for example by isolating an infected laptop from the network or disabling a stolen account.
- **Eradication**: remove the cause, such as malware, attacker accounts or the unpatched flaw.
- **Recovery**: restore systems from clean backups and watch closely for the attacker's return.
- **Lessons learned**: a blameless review of what happened and what to change.

Tying it all together is **defense in depth**: layered, independent controls, so that when one fails (and one always does), another still stands. Picture one phishing email. The filter misses it and the employee clicks. The password manager refuses to autofill on the lookalike domain; if the password is typed anyway, phishing-resistant MFA blocks the login. If malware runs instead, endpoint protection may catch it, least privilege limits what it reaches, central logging raises an alert and offline backups make recovery possible. No layer is perfect, but together they make an attacker's job slow, noisy and expensive.
sections.code:
One phishing email, many chances to stop it

  email filter              missed it
  security training         clicked anyway
  password manager          no autofill on the lookalike domain
  phishing-resistant MFA    login blocked
  endpoint protection       catches the malware
  least privilege           limits what it can reach
  central logging           alerts the security team
  offline backups           recovery without paying
sections.pitfall: Waiting for an incident to decide who to call and what to do. Without a plan, the first hours go to confusion while the attacker keeps working.

check.question: During an incident you find a laptop actively spreading malware to other machines. Which phase does "disconnect it from the network" belong to?
choices: Preparation
Containment
Eradication
Lessons learned
check.explanation: Isolating the laptop stops the spread without yet removing the cause, which is containment. Cleaning the malware off and closing the hole it used comes next, in eradication.

keyTerms.definition: Confidentiality, integrity and availability: the three goals security protects.
A weakness that a threat could exploit, such as an unpatched bug or a default password.
The likelihood that a threat exploits a vulnerability, combined with the impact if it does.
Manipulating people into giving up access, money or information; phishing is the most common form.
Malware that encrypts files and demands payment, often after stealing data too.
Proving who you are, versus deciding what you are allowed to do.
Multi-factor authentication: proof from different kinds of factor, such as a password plus a security key.
Trying username and password pairs leaked from one site on many others.
User input changing the structure of a SQL query because it was pasted into the query text.
Attacker-supplied script running in other users' browsers because output was not escaped.
Giving every person and program only the access it needs, for only as long as needed.
Layered, independent controls so that one failure does not mean a breach.

summary: Security protects confidentiality, integrity and availability, and risk is likelihood times impact.
Most attacks start with people; verify unusual requests through a channel you already trust.
Malware arrives through phishing, downloads and unpatched services; patching, least privilege and tested offline backups limit it.
Authentication proves who you are and authorization decides what you may do; use unique passwords, a manager and phishing-resistant MFA.
Keep data out of code: parameterized queries stop SQL injection and output escaping stops XSS.
Least privilege, fast patching, central logs, an incident plan and layered defenses turn breaches into contained incidents.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a non-technical coworker how one convincing phishing email could lead to a company-wide ransomware attack, and name at least four separate defenses that could each have stopped it.

questions.question: An attacker on the network secretly changes the amount in a bank transfer from 50 to 5,000 while it is in transit. Which security goal is broken?
choices: Confidentiality
Availability
Integrity
Authorization
questions.explanation: The data was altered without permission, which breaks integrity. Confidentiality would be broken if the attacker only read the transfer, and availability if the transfer could not go through at all.

questions.question: A company's public web server runs software with a known flaw that has not been patched. How should the flaw itself be classified?
choices: A vulnerability
A threat
An exploit
An incident
questions.explanation: An unpatched flaw is a weakness, which makes it a vulnerability. The threat is whoever might use it, the exploit is the technique they would use, and it only becomes an incident once someone actually does.

questions.question: What is the difference between a threat, a vulnerability and a risk?
questions.answer: A threat is someone or something that could cause harm. A vulnerability is a weakness it could use. Risk is how likely it is that the threat exploits the weakness, combined with how bad the damage would be.
questions.explanation: Real risk needs both pieces: a weakness nobody can reach is low risk, and a capable attacker with no weakness to use is also low risk.

questions.question: A logged-in employee opens the payroll page and gets an "access denied" error. Which check stopped them?
choices: Authentication
Encryption
Hashing
Authorization
questions.explanation: The employee is already logged in, so authentication succeeded. The system then decided this user is not allowed to view payroll, which is authorization.

questions.question: What is the three-letter acronym for logging in with two or more different kinds of proof, such as a password plus a code from your phone?
questions.explanation: MFA stands for multi-factor authentication. 2FA, two-factor authentication, is the common case of exactly two factors.

questions.question: Which login combination is true multi-factor authentication?
choices: A password plus the answer to a security question
A password plus a code from an authenticator app
A PIN plus a separate account password
A long password typed twice to confirm it
questions.explanation: A password is something you know and an app on your phone is something you have, so that is two different factors. A password plus a security question or PIN is still only something you know.

questions.question: This sign-up code stores a hash instead of the password. What is the security problem?
questions.code:
import hashlib

def save_user(db, username, password):
    digest = hashlib.md5(password.encode()).hexdigest()
    db.execute("INSERT INTO users VALUES (?, ?)", (username, digest))
choices: The INSERT statement is open to SQL injection
hexdigest() stores the password in readable form
MD5 is fast and unsalted, so leaked hashes crack quickly
Passwords should be encrypted instead so they can be recovered later
questions.explanation: MD5 is built for speed, so attackers can test billions of guesses per second, and without a salt, identical passwords produce identical hashes. Use a slow, salted password hash such as bcrypt or Argon2. The query is parameterized, so it is safe from injection, and passwords should never be recoverable.

questions.question: Attackers take email and password pairs leaked from one website and try them on banks and email providers. Which habit defeats this attack?
choices: A unique password for every site, stored in a password manager
Adding a new number to the end of your password each year
Clearing your browser cookies and history every day
Only logging in from your home network or work laptop
questions.explanation: This is credential stuffing, and it only works when a password is reused. A unique password per site means one leak unlocks only one account. Tweaking a reused password with a number is easy for attackers to guess.

questions.question: Which link really points to a site owned by example-bank.com?
choices: https://example-bank.com.secure-login.net/account
https://login.example-bank.com/account
https://example-bank-login.com/account
https://secure.example-bank.co/account
questions.explanation: Read the domain from the right, just before the first single slash: login.example-bank.com ends in example-bank.com. The first link is owned by secure-login.net, and the other two are different domains that only look similar.

questions.question: Someone calls claiming to be from IT, says your account is being attacked, and asks you to read out the MFA code you just received. What should you do?
choices: Read the code quickly, since the account is at risk
Give only the first half of the code, to be safe
Ask them for their employee ID, then read the code
Hang up and call IT back on a number you already know
questions.explanation: This is vishing. The code only arrived because the caller is trying to log in as you. Real IT staff never need your MFA code, and an employee ID is easy to fake, so verify through a channel you already trust.

questions.question: What is the name for phishing aimed at one specific person or team, using real details about them to look believable?
questions.explanation: Spear phishing is targeted phishing. Attackers research names, projects and suppliers so the message matches what the victim expects. When the target is a senior executive it is sometimes called whaling.

questions.question: Complete the sqlite3 query so the user's input is passed safely as a parameter.
questions.code:
name = input("Search name: ")
cur.execute("SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE name = _____", (name,))
choices: '{name}'
name
questions.explanation: sqlite3 uses ? as the placeholder and binds the tuple's values to it. A quoted '?' is just the literal text "?", '{name}' is a literal string because there is no f prefix, and a bare name would be read as a column name.

questions.question: A login form builds f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'". An attacker types ' OR '1'='1 as the name. What happens?
choices: The query fails with a syntax error and nothing is returned
The database escapes the quotes automatically
The WHERE clause becomes always true and every user row is returned
Only users literally named ' OR '1'='1 are returned
questions.explanation: The input closes the opening quote and appends OR '1'='1', which is true for every row, so the query returns the whole table. The database cannot escape anything here because the input is already part of the SQL text.

questions.question: This Flask search page works, but a security review flags it. What is the vulnerability?
choices: SQL injection, because q comes from the URL
Reflected XSS, because q goes into the HTML without escaping
The route must use POST instead of GET to be secure
request.args.get crashes if q is missing
questions.explanation: A link like /search?q=<script>...</script> makes the page run the attacker's script in the victim's browser. Escape q (or render a template with auto-escaping). There is no database query, so it is not SQL injection, and the default "" handles a missing q.

questions.question: Complete the function so a user's comment is shown as text instead of being run as HTML.
choices: html.unescape
str.strip
repr
html.escape
questions.explanation: html.escape turns characters like < and > into < and >, so the browser displays them instead of treating them as tags. html.unescape does the opposite and would make the problem worse.

questions.question: A web shop only needs to read products and create orders. Which database account should the app use?
choices: A dedicated account allowed to read products and insert orders
The database admin account, so no query ever fails on permissions
A shared account that every internal app also uses
An account with full rights to the shop's database
questions.explanation: Least privilege: if the app is compromised, the attacker only gets what the app's account can do. With an admin or full-rights account, one SQL injection bug could drop tables or read every other database.

questions.question: A vendor releases a patch for a vulnerability in your internet-facing VPN, and attackers are already exploiting it. What is the best response?
choices: Wait for the next quarterly maintenance window
Apply the patch urgently, ahead of routine updates
Rely on antivirus to catch any attack
Hide the VPN's version number from its login page
questions.explanation: An actively exploited bug on an internet-facing system is the highest priority, because attackers scan for it within hours. Waiting leaves it open, and hiding the version number does not remove the flaw.

questions.question: Match each incident to the part of the CIA triad it mainly breaks.

pairs.left: A DDoS attack keeps the shop offline for a day
A stolen, unencrypted laptop exposes customer records
Malware quietly changes the bank details on invoices

questions.explanation: Ask what went wrong for the data: could not be reached (availability), was read by the wrong people (confidentiality), or was changed without permission (integrity).

questions.question: Which control reduces risk mainly by lowering the likelihood of an incident, rather than its impact?
choices: Keeping tested offline backups
Buying a cyber insurance policy
Requiring MFA for every remote login
Encrypting the disks of company laptops
questions.explanation: MFA makes a stolen password far less likely to turn into a break-in. Backups and disk encryption limit the damage once something has happened (lost files come back, a stolen laptop stays unreadable), and insurance transfers the cost.

questions.question: Which of these are red flags in an email? Select all that apply.
choices: Pressure to act within the hour or lose access
A link whose real domain differs from the company it claims to be
A request to pay a new bank account, skipping the usual approval
Your manager's correct name and job title in the signature
The message arrived during normal working hours
questions.explanation: Urgency, a mismatched domain and a request to bypass process are classic signs. Correct names and normal timing prove nothing either way: attackers look those details up.

questions.question: An email from the CFO's real mailbox, which attackers have taken over, asks accounts payable to urgently switch a supplier's bank details. It passes every email authentication check. What still stops the fraud?
choices: Checking that the message passed SPF and DKIM before paying
Replying to the CFO's email to ask whether the request is real
Reading the message closely for spelling and grammar mistakes
Calling the supplier on a number already on file before any change
questions.explanation: The mailbox is genuine, so email checks pass and a reply goes straight to the attacker. A process that confirms payment changes through an independent, known channel stops the fraud no matter how convincing the email is.

questions.question: Match each kind of malware to its behavior.

pairs.right: Attaches to files and spreads when they are run
Spreads across networks by itself, with no user action
Poses as useful software so the victim installs it
Encrypts files and demands payment for the key
Secretly collects information such as keystrokes

questions.explanation: Virus, worm and trojan describe how malware spreads or gets installed; ransomware and spyware describe what it does once inside. One sample can be several at once.

questions.question: Which setup best ensures you can recover from ransomware without paying?
choices: A cloud folder that syncs every change instantly
A strong antivirus product on every laptop
Tested backups kept offline or immutable, separate from the network
A second copy of the files on the same server
questions.explanation: Ransomware encrypts whatever it can reach, including synced folders and copies on the same server. Backups it cannot reach, and that you have actually restored from, are what let you recover. Antivirus helps prevent infection but guarantees nothing.

questions.question: WannaCry encrypted files for ransom and spread between computers by itself through an unpatched Windows file-sharing flaw, with no clicks needed. Which two categories describe it?
choices: Spyware and trojan
Virus and rootkit
Adware and keylogger
Ransomware and worm
questions.explanation: Encrypting files for payment makes it ransomware, and spreading across the network on its own makes it a worm. The patch for the flaw it used had been released two months earlier.

questions.question: An attacker has a user's password and keeps triggering MFA push requests until the tired user taps Approve. Which method best resists this and real-time phishing sites?
choices: SMS one-time codes sent to the user's phone
A passkey or FIDO2 security key bound to the real site's domain
Security questions about the user's first pet
A longer password that changes every 30 days
questions.explanation: A passkey signs in only for the genuine domain and needs the user's device, so there is no code to relay and no push to approve by mistake. SMS codes can be phished or SIM-swapped, and security questions are just more things you know.

questions.question: Put these ways of protecting an account in order from weakest to strongest.
items: A password reused on several other sites
A unique, long password from a password manager
A unique password plus a code sent by SMS
A unique password plus an authenticator app code
A passkey or hardware security key
questions.explanation: Reuse falls to credential stuffing. A unique password fixes that, a second factor stops stolen passwords, app codes avoid SIM swapping, and passkeys also resist phishing because they only work on the real domain.

questions.question: This code uses psycopg2, whose placeholder is written %s. Is the query safe?
choices: Yes, because %s is the driver's placeholder
No: the % operator builds the SQL string before the driver sees it
Yes, as long as order_id comes from the URL path
No, because psycopg2 does not support placeholders
questions.explanation: Python's % operator pastes order_id into the text first, so the driver receives finished SQL and injection is possible. Pass the value separately instead: cur.execute("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = %s", (order_id,)).
questions.concept: string formatting is not a parameter

questions.question: Which of these help defend against cross-site scripting? Select all that apply.
choices: Escaping output for the HTML context it is written into
A template engine with automatic escaping, such as Jinja
A Content-Security-Policy header limiting which scripts run
Switching the form from GET to POST
Hashing users' passwords with bcrypt
questions.explanation: XSS is stopped where input meets HTML: escape it, preferably automatically, and add CSP as a second layer. The HTTP method and password hashing are unrelated to whether a script can be injected into a page.

questions.question: Why do administrators use a separate privileged account instead of their everyday one?
choices: So phishing or malware on their everyday account cannot use admin rights
Because admin accounts are technically unable to open or read email
So that every login takes longer, which discourages careless mistakes
Because company policy allows each person only one password per account
questions.explanation: The everyday account is the one exposed to phishing links and malicious downloads. Keeping admin rights on a separate account, used only for admin work, means a compromise of the daily account does not hand over the keys.

questions.question: This cloud policy is attached to a nightly job that only uploads backup files to the bucket nightly-backups. What is the problem?
choices: The Version date is too old to grant any storage permissions at all
Effect must be set to Deny for jobs that run unattended at night
It allows every S3 action everywhere; the job needs only s3:PutObject on that bucket
Policies must list every file name the job will upload to the bucket
questions.explanation: With s3:* on *, anyone who compromises the job can read, delete or overwrite every bucket in the account. Least privilege means Action s3:PutObject and Resource arn:aws:s3:::nightly-backups/* only.

questions.question: What is a zero-day vulnerability?
choices: A flaw that is fixed on the same day it is reported
A bug that only affects systems with zero users
A vulnerability scored 0 out of 10 for severity
A flaw attackers exploit before the vendor has released a fix
questions.explanation: Defenders have had "zero days" to patch it. Once a fix ships, the flaw becomes a known vulnerability, and unpatched systems are the main target.

questions.question: Which steps reduce a new server's attack surface? Select all that apply.
choices: Changing or disabling default passwords
Turning off services and ports it does not need
Applying security updates before exposing it to the internet
Installing extra tools in case they are useful later
Allowing SSH logins as root with a password
questions.explanation: Fewer accounts with known passwords, fewer listening services and no known holes mean fewer ways in. Extra software adds attack surface, and root password logins invite brute-force attacks.

questions.question: Put the incident response phases in order.
questions.explanation: Prepare before anything happens, detect and scope the incident, contain the spread, remove the cause, restore service, then learn from it. In practice teams loop back when they find more affected systems.

questions.question: Why should servers send their logs to a central system instead of only keeping them locally?
choices: An attacker with admin rights can wipe local logs, but not copies already sent elsewhere
Local logs are always encrypted, so nobody can read them
Central logging makes the servers themselves run faster
Laws forbid storing logs on the server that produced them
questions.explanation: Covering tracks by deleting logs is a standard attacker move. A central copy survives it, and it also lets you correlate events across many systems, such as one IP failing logins on every server.
